## Overview

EcologicalCellularAutomata collects published cellular automata for plant
diseases and pests. Each model is a CellularAutomataCore `CAModel`, so it runs
with the core's schemes, backends, callbacks and ensembles. Each also carries
metadata: its source, what the source compared it with, and how faithfully it
follows the source. This vignette shows how to find a model, read what it is
and is not, build it, and run it.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## Finding a model

```{julia}
list_models()
```

The models can be filtered by category or by fidelity:

```{julia}
(diseases=list_models(; category="plant disease"),
 pests=list_models(; category="agricultural pest"),
 reproductions=list_models(; fidelity=:reproduction))
```

## What a model is, and is not

`model_info` returns the metadata of a model:

```{julia}
info = model_info(:fungus_dispersal)
```

The fidelity says how close the model is to its source. A *reproduction* is
the source's model with the source's parameters. An *adaptation* fills gaps
in the source, or departs from it, and lists every such choice. An *inspired*
model takes only the source's ideas. Even a reproduction makes choices where
its source is silent:

```{julia}
foreach(d -> println("- ", d), info.deviations)
```

A table of the whole zoo:

```{julia}
for id in list_models()
    m = model_info(id)
    println(rpad(id, 22), rpad(m.fidelity, 14), m.organism)
end
```

## Building and running a model

`build` returns the model, with the source's parameter values as defaults:

```{julia}
model = build(:fungus_dispersal)
```

`problem` returns a problem with the source's setup: here a 60 × 60 field with
nine infectious hosts in the middle, for 120 days. Keywords change the setup,
and `pmap` changes parameters by name:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:fungus_dispersal; seed=1)
sol = solve(prob; saveat=40)
plot([heatmap(u.host'; c=[:palegreen, :orange, :darkred], clims=(0, 2), colorbar=false,
              aspect_ratio=:equal, framestyle=:none, title="day $t")
      for (t, u) in zip(sol.t, sol.u)]...; layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

Healthy hosts are green, latent hosts orange and infectious hosts dark red.
Changing a parameter, here halving the daily propagule load:

```{julia}
half = solve(problem(:fungus_dispersal; seed=1, pmap=(; load=20.0)); save_everystep=false)
(full_load=fungus_infected(sol.u[end]), half_load=fungus_infected(half.u[end]))
```

## Replicates

The models are stochastic, and a single run says little. Most problem
constructors draw their initial state from `seed` as well, so replicates are
problems built with different seeds. Here the infected hosts at day 120 over
ten replicates:

```{julia}
finals = [fungus_infected(solve(problem(:fungus_dispersal; seed=s);
                                save_everystep=false).u[end]) for s in 1:10]
(mean=mean(finals), sd=round(std(finals); digits=1))
```

The core's `EnsembleProblem` runs replicates in parallel. Its `prob_func`
builds each replicate's problem from SciMLBase's ensemble context, whose
`sim_id` numbers the replicates:

```{julia}
ens = EnsembleProblem(problem(:rhizoctonia_contact);
                      prob_func=(prob, ctx) -> problem(:rhizoctonia_contact; seed=ctx.sim_id))
runs = solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=50, save_everystep=false)
mean(rhizoctonia_infected(r.u[end]) for r in runs.u)
```

## Any backend

A model is specified once. The core's backends run it, and those that support
it agree exactly, because every random number comes from a counter-based
generator keyed by the seed, the cell, the time and a draw number. The
viral front model on three backends:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:domany_kinzel_viral; L=2000, tspan=200, seed=3)
threaded = solve(prob; backend=ArrayBackend(), save_everystep=false).u[end]
serial = solve(prob; backend=ArrayBackend(; threaded=false), save_everystep=false).u[end]
reference = solve(prob; backend=ReferenceBackend(), save_everystep=false).u[end]
threaded == serial == reference
```

## Models with callbacks

Some sources describe steps that no local rule can express. Mites in the
Huffaker model act one at a time, and their moves write two cells. Insecticide
in the Bt cotton model is sprayed when either pest reaches a share of the whole
field. Such parts are callbacks stored with the problem, so `solve` runs them
without being told:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:bt_cotton_refuge; n=200, initial=50, scenario=:insecticide)
keys(prob.kwargs)
```

They draw their random numbers from a generator seeded by the problem's seed
and the time, so a run is reproducible:

```{julia}
a = solve(prob; save_everystep=false).u[end]
b = solve(prob; save_everystep=false).u[end]
a == b
```

The following vignettes take the models one at a time. Each compares the
model with its source's results and repeats its deviations.
